title: 2026 In-House Legal AI Report: Legal AI Is Everywhere. Now Comes the Hard Part.
pub: Axiom (survey fielded by InsightDynamo, commissioned by Axiom); press release via PR Newswire
author: Axiom

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: Axiom accepts the cluster’s core claim that legal departments can capture AI gains only through organisational absorption, and materially strengthens it with survey evidence on weak scaling and ROI measurement plus concrete practices for ownership, training, governance, focused pilots and outcome measurement. It also supports the cluster’s caution that benefits remain concentrated in document-heavy tasks and have rarely translated into outside-counsel rate relief.
qs: The departments pulling ahead built structure instead: someone owns the program, pilots have defined goals, and results get reviewed before the program expands.

- **The payoff is real but narrow - and it isn't reaching outside counsel rates.** AI is delivering ROI, but mainly in a handful of high-volume, document-heavy tasks: legal research, contract review, and document summarization.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: Axiom reinforces the cluster’s claim that tool access and rising adoption do not by themselves produce effective transformation. Its international in-house survey materially extends that proposition with concrete evidence of weak ROI measurement, limited organisation-wide scaling and workforce capability gaps, while recommending sustained investment in people and change management. It does not directly address verification or apprenticeship risks.
qs: Change management is not a        We commissioned a survey of 528 in-house legal leaders           one-time communications task.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: Axiom accepts the cluster’s core view that AI value depends on operating discipline rather than software access alone, while adding concrete implementation practices, evidence that returns remain concentrated in selected workflows, and buyer preferences favouring ALSPs. Its evidence on unrealised outside-counsel rate relief also reinforces the cluster’s caution that pricing and bargaining shifts are emerging rather than complete, though Axiom’s provider claims are partly promotional.
qs: The departments pulling ahead built structure instead: someone owns the program, pilots have defined goals, and results get reviewed before the program expands.

Asked who they'd trust for it, respondents rank alternative legal service providers (ALSPs) ahead of consulting firms, law firms, AI vendors, and industry associations - and prefer ALSPs over law firms for AI-enabled work by more than two to one (52% to 24%).

st.t: Value capture: Integrated delivery reshapes market boundaries
st.an: Axiom accepts that AI-created value depends on integrated delivery capabilities rather than technology access alone, and materially develops the cluster through workflow-specific governance recommendations and survey evidence that buyers prefer ALSPs for AI-enabled guidance and work. Its provider-preference findings indicate buyer pressure and possible shifts in value capture, but do not demonstrate actual provider performance or market-wide outcomes.
qs: Asked who they'd trust for it, respondents rank alternative legal service providers (ALSPs) ahead of consulting firms, law firms, AI vendors, and industry associations - and prefer ALSPs over law firms for AI-enabled work by more than two to one (52% to 24%).
Are AI-enabled workflows being measured against legal outcomes, or only usage metrics?

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Axiom accepts the cluster’s core proposition and materially extends it with in-house survey evidence and an implementation playbook. It locates returns in a narrow set of document-heavy tasks and argues that workflow integration, training, governance, measurement and human supervision—not software acquisition alone—determine realised value. Its evidence is primarily self-reported and commercially commissioned, with illustrative case studies rather than causal proof.
qs: - **The payoff is real but narrow - and it isn't reaching outside counsel rates.** AI is delivering ROI, but mainly in a handful of high-volume, document-heavy tasks: legal research, contract review, and document summarization.
What ranks first is strong integration with existing workflows.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: Axiom’s description of on-demand lawyers, project support and embedded teams supports the cluster’s account of buyers using ALSPs and flexible delivery models alongside law firms. Its claimed lower cost and AI-enabled scale are consistent with competitive pressure on traditional delivery, but the excerpt is promotional and provides no substantive evidence on workflow-level allocation, pricing reform, junior training or verification risks.

kp.k: Commissioned survey captures large-company legal leaders’ reported experiences
kp.d: InsightDynamo conducted Axiom’s online survey of 528 in-house legal leaders between March 13 and March 25, 2026, across Australia, Canada, Hong Kong, Singapore, the United Kingdom and the United States. Respondents’ companies had annual revenue of at least $100 million; 77% had revenue of $1 billion or more. The report states that data were tested for statistical significance at a 95% confidence interval. Its disclaimer limits findings to surveyed respondents, identifies self-reporting and sampling limitations, distinguishes Axiom’s editorial interpretation, and describes customer cases as illustrative.
qs: including sampling variability, respondent interpretation, and self-reporting bias.
Any customer examples or case studies described herein are illustrative only.
Individual client results may vary depending on facts, circumstances, implementation

kp.k: Widespread adoption does not mean organization-wide optimization
kp.d: The report states that 82% of surveyed teams use AI in some form and 18% have not started. It headlines a 7% optimization rate, although the adoption-stage chart lists 30 optimizing respondents within the 431 AI users, alongside 113 exploring, 75 piloting, 125 expanding usage, 65 using multiple applications and 23 struggling with broad adoption. Regional charts, also covering AI users, report optimization at 10% in the Americas, 5% in the UK and 3% in APAC. The press release’s characterization of only 7% having made AI work is broader than the chart’s optimization category.
qs: Few Have
Mastered It.
Legal AI is Everywhere, but Only 7% of Legal Teams Have Made It Work
Optimizing AI Usage

kp.k: AI budgets rise despite weak outcome measurement
kp.d: All 431 AI-using teams expect budgets to increase next cycle; none plan cuts, and 81% plan increases of at least 10%. These are spending intentions, not observed future expenditure. Budget size varies with organizational scale: 23% of teams with 31–50 lawyers and 44% with 51 or more report budgets of at least $1 million, compared with 5% of teams with 1–15 lawyers and 6% with 16–30. The report contrasts this investment with limited formal ROI measurement.
qs: Every in-house legal team using AI plans to spend more on it next year.
Eighty-three percent cannot show whether last year's spending paid off.
Legal AI Budgets

kp.k: Reported ROI largely reflects perceptions rather than established metrics
kp.d: Among 431 AI users, 17% have established ROI metrics, 51% measure informally or inconsistently, 29% have measurement in development and 3% have no ability to measure. The report explicitly presents subsequent ROI findings as perceptions rather than measured outcomes. Formally measuring teams emphasize internal labor costs and time saved per task; informal measurement emphasizes adoption and satisfaction. Perceived value concentrates in legal research, contract drafting/review/analysis and document summarization, and more skilled teams report stronger perceived returns. These findings do not establish causal effects of skills on returns.

Approaches, Two Different
Views of AI ROI
ROI built on anecdotes is not ROI.

kp.k: Tool uncertainty outweighs budget among surveyed non-adopters
kp.d: Among 97 non-adopters, 63% cite uncertainty about appropriate tools, 51% lack clear evidence of positive ROI, 41% cite privacy or confidentiality concerns and 35% lack a clear business case. Funding is cited by 25%, leadership prioritization by 22%, and accuracy or reliability concerns by 8%. Separately, corporate IT controls tool selection and pilots at 70% of AI-using teams, compared with 29% for legal operations. Axiom frames this allocation of control outside Legal as a structural accountability problem for GCs.
qs: In most legal departments, someone outside Legal picks the AI tools.
For GCs accountable for outcomes, that's a structural problem, not a software problem.
No clear evidence for positive ROI
Lack of internal budget or funding

kp.k: General-purpose deployment creates demand for legal-specific configuration
kp.d: The report identifies ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini as the most widely used tools and says 67% of teams running these platforms use general-purpose rather than legal-specific configurations. It reports average year-over-year growth of 107% for the top four general-purpose tools versus 44% for the top six legal-specific tools. Axiom argues that legal suitability requires configuration, prompts, workflow design and review protocols beyond the software itself; this is its interpretation of the implementation gap.
qs: Two-thirds of legal teams are running general-purpose AI in its default configuration.
The three most widely used AI tools in legal - ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini - were not built for legal work, and most teams haven't configured them to behave as if they were.
General-Purpose AI
Legal-Specific

kp.k: Training and regular use lag behind software access
kp.d: Among AI-using teams, 59% rate skills as intermediate and 10% as advanced; 40% identify skills gaps as a major barrier. The report says 91% of team members received ten hours or less of AI-specific training in the preceding 12 months, including 52% receiving two to five hours. Only 17% of teams report a majority of lawyers using licensed tools daily, and 25% report majority monthly use. Axiom recommends ongoing training and change management rather than treating tool access or initial onboarding as sufficient.
qs: Training hasn't kept pace either: most lawyers still aren't regularly using tools their own departments have already paid for.
Treat training and change management as an ongoing investment, not a one-time onboarding task.
Prioritize Training and Change Management

kp.k: Structured evaluation and pilots remain uncommon
kp.d: Before commitment, 11% of AI-using teams report rigorous evaluation, 77% moderate evaluation and 12% light evaluation relying primarily on vendor demonstrations. Pilot approaches are 23% structured, 61% semi-structured and 15% informal. Most pilots last three to six months. Axiom recommends eight-to-twelve-week pilots with a focused, low-risk use case, baseline measurement and a clear decision at completion; the proposed duration is advice, not an experimentally demonstrated optimum. SMBC’s Hiro Oshima separately endorses rigorous evaluation grounded in actual workflows and risk environments.
qs: Think eight to twelve weeks, one use case, and measurement baked in from day one.
Without a definition of success, a pilot produces activity, not insights.
The real test is whether a solution can deliver reliable value in the workflows, risk environment, and business context where legal teams operate.

kp.k: Axiom emphasizes governance and implementation over tool acquisition
kp.d: Axiom organizes its recommendations around people, focused pilots, early governance, outcome measurement and external assistance. Across most governance practices, roughly four in ten teams report implementation and four in ten planning; practices include peer review, output quality assurance, accuracy audits, policies and workflow integration. Retrospectively, 37% would improve measurement, 36% build internal expertise and 35% evaluate tools more rigorously. The five principles derive from 384 open-ended responses categorized with AI. Axiom’s claim that discipline separates successful teams from others is an editorial synthesis of this survey, not a demonstrated causal comparison.
qs: Ranking based on 384 open-ended responses, analyzed, and categorized with AI. (N = 384)
Establish AI governance and policies before deployment - not after problems surface.
The teams pulling ahead aren't spending more than everyone else—they've simply stopped treating AI as a side project.
There's clear ownership, real training, and someone accountable for the results before anything scales.

kp.k: External guidance demand favors alternative legal service providers
kp.d: Outside tool-selection guidance would help 98% of current AI users and 77% of non-adopters; 96% of current users say they would use an ALSP for adoption or implementation. Respondents rank ALSPs ahead of other guidance sources and prefer them to law firms for AI-enabled work, 52% versus 24%. The report says frequently outsourced applications overlap with perceived internal ROI leaders: high-volume contract review, research and summarization. These are reported preferences and willingness, not measured shifts in market share. Axiom presents the findings while itself offering ALSP services.
qs: 98% of current AI users and 77% of teams that haven't adopted AI yet say outside guidance on tool selection would help.
prefer ALSPs over law firms for AI-enabled work by more than two to one (52% to 24%).
The highest-return AI work is being sent out.

kp.k: Clients expect AI-related reductions in outside counsel rates
kp.d: The report says 95% of in-house teams expect outside counsel to use AI, while 92% expect or negotiate AI-related rate cuts. The detailed chart reports 34% actively negotiating reductions, 58% expecting reductions without always obtaining them and 7% not addressing billing rates. Axiom characterizes savings as mostly not reaching clients. In a customer quotation carried by Axiom, Nexora GC Lisa Lischak describes turning first to ALSPs because some traditional law firms exhibit risk aversion or billing incentives that reward automatable work.
qs: 92% of in-house teams expect or are negotiating AI-related rate cuts from outside counsel.
Few are getting them.
billing that still rewards work ripe for automation.

kp.k: Customer cases pair AI processing with human verification
kp.d: Axiom’s healthcare case reports migrating 344 supplier contracts with a senior lawyer using Legora, followed by cross-checking against client records, correcting entity data and determining required agreements. It claims 70% lower migration spend using an average in-house compensation versus subscription-and-team-structure comparison. A manufacturer case describes reviewing more than 16,000 legacy agreements, isolating approximately 1,500 with change-in-control language, manually validating AI classifications and mapping 185 unfavorable contract families. These examples describe lawyer-in-the-loop delivery rather than direct reliance on unverified AI output.
qs: Lawyers always in the loop.
reviewed the agreements and manually validated classifications for accuracy.

kp.k: AI-enabled staffing supports reported headcount avoidance and capacity gains
kp.d: In Axiom’s energy-services vignette, budget constraints prompted two employee departures before an experienced Axiom attorney developed DraftPilot contract playbooks and trained staff. Axiom reports 50% shorter average review time, three AI-enabled attorneys matching four attorneys’ output, one FTE-equivalent capacity gain and $220,000 annual savings. The savings footnote compares actual Axiom rates with law-firm equivalents, rather than isolating AI’s effect. A separate pharmaceutical case reports seven lawyers and one project manager at peak supporting a new digital business across four legal functions without permanent hires.

kp.k: Migration cases illustrate gains with differing comparison baselines
kp.d: An aerospace customer vignette reports six weeks of data cleanup and backend reconfiguration before Legora-supported migration of 1,400 contracts into Ironclad. Axiom claims 20–30% higher accuracy than the client’s existing CMS AI tool in a head-to-head comparison and 63% fewer project hours than traditional manual-processing benchmarks. A medical-equipment vignette reports one dedicated week to upload and tag more than 750 contracts, extracting 10–15 clauses each, compared with an estimated three months of paralegal work alongside other duties. The latter comparison combines AI use with dedicated staffing rather than representing equal staffing conditions.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Axiom claims that AI is becoming standard in corporate legal departments, but realized value depends on disciplined implementation rather than simply buying tools or increasing budgets.
pts.d: Axiom reports 82% adoption among surveyed departments and rising budgets among all 431 current AI users, while only 17% have established ROI metrics. Its adoption-stage chart identifies 30 respondents, or 7% of the AI-user subgroup, as optimizing AI across their department; the overview and press release describe this more broadly as 7% of legal teams. Axiom and Sara Morgan attribute successful scaling to ownership, focused pilots, training, governance, workflow configuration and measurement. They present this as a reproducible operating approach. The report also claims that corporate IT controls tool selection in 70% of AI-using departments, that general-purpose tools dominate and are frequently not configured for legal work, and that training and regular usage lag licensing. It reports average year-on-year growth of 107% for its top four general-purpose tools versus 44% for its top six legal-specific tools. Perceived returns concentrate in legal research, contract review and document summarization, and rise with reported team skill. Axiom further claims that AI creates demand for outside implementation services and opportunities for ALSPs: 98% of users want tool-selection guidance, 96% would use an ALSP for adoption or implementation, and respondents prefer ALSPs over law firms for AI-enabled work by 52% to 24%. It describes pressure for lower outside-counsel rates without commensurate realized rate reductions. Its client examples and product claims describe faster document work, lower costs and greater capacity without proportional permanent hiring, with lawyers remaining involved.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines commissioned survey findings, executives’ interpretations and recommendations, and illustrative Axiom client cases; it distinguishes reported perceptions from measured outcomes.
pts.d: InsightDynamo surveyed 528 in-house legal leaders online for Axiom. Companies had at least $100 million in annual revenue, and 77% had revenue of at least $1 billion. Many deployment, budget and provider-preference findings use the 431 AI-user respondents; non-adopter findings use 97 respondents. The five principles derive from 384 open-ended responses categorized with AI, alongside Axiom's interpretation. The report explicitly says its ROI section concerns perceptions rather than measured outcomes: formal-metric teams number 73 and informal-measurement teams 221. The asserted importance of discipline over spending is Axiom's synthesis, not a separately described causal experiment. Illustrative cases include: 344 healthcare supplier contracts migrated with a claimed 70% spending reduction, calculated against average in-house compensation and an AI-enabled subscription/consolidated-team model; an energy company reporting review time halved, three AI-enabled attorneys matching four attorneys' output, and $220,000 annual savings, with the stated cost comparison using Axiom rates versus law-firm equivalents; 1,400 aerospace contracts migrated with claimed 20–30% higher accuracy than the client's CMS AI tool and 63% fewer project hours against manual-processing benchmarks; a manufacturer reviewing more than 16,000 agreements with manual validation; and a medical-equipment company completing 750-plus contracts in one dedicated week versus an estimated three months of internal paralegal capacity alongside other duties. These examples combine tooling, experienced staff, workflow redesign and sometimes dedicated capacity. Axiom's product section additionally advertises 40–60% faster contract review and 20–60% task-time savings as reported by its talent, and large-scale review and diligence up to 4–10 times faster at approximately 50% lower cost. These are provider claims, not survey-wide measured results. Named executive comments supply professional interpretation rather than additional quantified tests.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The source describes adoption at the March 2026 survey date, budget intentions for the next cycle, and implementation-dependent gains rather than an unconditional forecast of autonomous legal practice.
pts.d: The survey was fielded March 13–25, 2026, and the accompanying release is dated July 9, 2026. Budget increases are respondent intentions for the next budget cycle, described in the release as next year, not completed expenditure. Tool-growth comparisons are labeled year-on-year, and training questions concern the preceding 12 months. Axiom recommends eight-to-twelve-week pilots with one focused, low-risk use case and measurement from the outset, rather than the commonly reported three-to-six-month pilots. This duration is a recommendation, not an experimentally established threshold. Claimed gains depend on tool suitability and legal-specific configuration, structured source data, governance, ongoing training, workflow integration, defined outcomes and human review. Case timelines are project-specific: six weeks to extend energy-company playbooks, six weeks of aerospace data cleanup, and a one-week dedicated diligence engagement. Annual savings in the energy vignette should be distinguished from project-duration savings elsewhere. The source limits its survey claims to respondents rather than the entire legal industry and describes cases as illustrative and context-dependent.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are enterprise legal buyers, their lawyers and legal operations teams, corporate IT, outside law firms and ALSPs supplying AI-enabled work.
pts.d: The surveyed buyer population consists of CLOs, GCs, deputies, other senior counsel and legal operations leaders in Australia, Canada, Hong Kong, Singapore, the United Kingdom and the United States, predominantly at billion-dollar enterprises. GCs face responsibility for outcomes even where IT selects tools; lawyers need sustained training and remain responsible for verification and judgment; legal operations teams support governance, migration and workflow design. Smaller departments are particularly dependent on IT selection, while larger teams report substantially larger AI budgets. Axiom presents ALSPs, including itself, as providers of experienced talent and implementation services that bridge the gap between software licensing and useful legal delivery. Law firms face buyer expectations for AI use, rate reductions and competition for high-volume document work. AI vendors supply software but are distinguished from ALSPs delivering the work. Client cases suggest selective substitution for additional or replacement staffing, not a general prediction that lawyers disappear: the energy vignette reports maintaining output without conventional backfilling, while other cases free internal capacity or obtain specialist support without permanent hires. The manufacturer and healthcare cases explicitly retain human checking of AI output. The source concerns enterprise service delivery and cost savings, not access to justice or population-wide legal employment displacement.
